units.title: Complex sentences
units.intro: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

cards.title: Independent and dependent clauses
rule: An **independent clause** can stand alone as a sentence: *Students revise every evening.*
A **dependent (subordinate) clause** cannot stand alone: *because the exam is near*.
Join them without a comma splice: *Students revise every evening **because** the exam is near.*

examples.text: She left early because she felt ill.
Because she felt ill.
examples.fix: Because she felt ill, she left early.

examples.text: She left early, she felt ill.
examples.fix: She left early because she felt ill.

cards.title: Finite and non-finite clauses
rule: A **finite clause** has a tensed verb: *when he **arrives***.
A **non-finite clause** uses infinitive, -ing, or -ed with no tense: *to arrive early*, *arriving early*, *surprised by the news*.
Non-finite clauses keep writing compact for essays and reports.

examples.text: Hoping to win, they trained harder.
Hope to win, they trained harder.
examples.fix: Hoping to win, they trained harder.

examples.text: To finish on time is important.

units.title: Relative clauses
units.intro: Relative clauses add information about a noun using who, which, that, whose, where, when.

cards.title: Defining vs non-defining
rule: A **defining** relative clause identifies which person/thing: *The student **who arrived late** missed the quiz.* (no commas)
A **non-defining** clause adds extra information about an already clear noun: *Asmara, **which is the capital**, is cool in July.* (commas)
Do not use **that** in non-defining clauses.

examples.text: The book that I borrowed is new.
Asmara, that is the capital, is cool.
examples.fix: Asmara, which is the capital, is cool.

examples.text: My brother, who lives in Keren, called.

cards.title: Whose, where, when
rule: **whose** = possession: *the teacher whose class we joined*
**where** = place: *the school where we study*
**when** = time: *the year when Eritrea became independent*

the girl who bag was lost

units.title: Conditionals (mixed and review)
units.intro: Review types 0–3, then mix time references for past cause + present result.

cards.title: Types 0–3 in brief
rule: **0** facts: *If you heat ice, it melts.* (present + present)
**1** real future: *If it rains, we will stay in.* (present + will)
**2** unreal present: *If I had time, I would help.* (past + would)
**3** unreal past: *If she had revised, she would have passed.* (had + would have)

If I will see her, I tell her.

cards.title: Mixed conditionals
rule: Past cause → present result: *If I **had studied** medicine, I **would be** a doctor now.*
Present (ongoing) cause → past result: *If she **were** more careful, she **would not have broken** it.*
Keep the if-clause and main clause times consistent with the meaning you intend.

units.title: Advanced passives and reporting
units.intro: Passives shift focus to the action or receiver; reporting verbs introduce other people’s words or views.

cards.title: Passive with modals and perfects
rule: Modal + be + past participle: *The essay **must be submitted** today.*
Perfect passive: *The results **have been published**.* / *The room **had been cleaned**.*
Use passive when the doer is unknown, obvious, or less important.

examples.text: The work must be finished by Friday.
The work must finished by Friday.
examples.fix: The work must be finished by Friday.

examples.text: The notices have been posted.

cards.title: Reporting verbs and structures
rule: Say/tell/ask + clause: *She said (that) she was ready.* / *He told us to wait.*
Suggest/recommend + -ing or that-clause: *They suggested revising together.*
Claim/argue/insist that… are useful in formal essays.

examples.text: He told me to arrive early.
He said me to arrive early.
examples.fix: He told me to arrive early. / He said (that) I should arrive early.

examples.text: The writer argues that literacy builds opportunity.

units.title: Nominalisation and formal register
units.intro: Academic writing often turns verbs and adjectives into nouns (nominalisation) and prefers formal vocabulary.

cards.title: Nominalisation
rule: Verb → noun: *decide → decision*, *develop → development*, *fail → failure*.
Adjective → noun: *important → importance*, *possible → possibility*.
Nominal style: *The **rapid expansion** of towns creates pressure on services.*

examples.text: Their decision surprised everyone.
They decide surprised everyone.
The importance of literacy is clear.

cards.title: Formal vs informal
rule: Prefer precise verbs: *obtain, require, demonstrate* over *get, need, show* in formal essays.
Avoid chatty fillers (*well, you know, lots of*) and contractions in formal exams.
Keep a respectful tone: *Could you clarify…?* rather than *What do you want?*

examples.text: The study demonstrates a clear trend.
The study shows stuff pretty well.
examples.fix: The study demonstrates a clear trend.

examples.text: Candidates are required to arrive early.

units.title: Cohesion and discourse markers
units.intro: Cohesion links sentences so the paragraph reads as one argument, not a list of facts.

cards.title: Discourse markers
rule: Addition: *moreover, furthermore, in addition*
Contrast: *however, nevertheless, on the other hand*
Cause/result: *therefore, consequently, as a result*
Example/clarifying: *for instance, that is, in other words*

examples.text: The roads flooded; therefore schools closed.
The roads flooded; however schools closed.
examples.fix: The roads flooded; therefore schools closed.

examples.text: Moreover, attendance improved after the campaign.

cards.title: Reference and lexical cohesion
rule: Use pronouns carefully: *this / these / such* to point back to a clear noun idea.
Repeat key nouns or use synonyms to keep the topic visible.
Avoid vague *this* when the reader cannot see what it refers to.

examples.text: Pollution rose. This increase worried officials.
Pollution rose. This worried.
examples.fix: Pollution rose. This increase worried officials.

examples.text: Farmers and growers both need water.

head: Wrong

units.title: Verb patterns: gerunds and infinitives
units.intro: After some verbs you must use -ing; after others to + verb; a few allow both with a meaning change.

cards.title: Common patterns
rule: **enjoy / avoid / suggest / finish / keep** + -ing: *She enjoys reading.*
**want / decide / hope / plan / afford** + to-infinitive: *They decided to wait.*
**stop + -ing** = quit a habit; **stop + to-infinitive** = pause in order to do something.

examples.text: He suggested revising together.
He suggested to revise together.
We stopped to rest.

cards.title: Adjective + infinitive; preposition + -ing
rule: *easy / hard / important / ready* + to-infinitive: *It is important to listen.*
After a preposition use -ing: *interested in learning*, *good at solving*, *before leaving*.

examples.text: She is interested in studying history.
She is interested in to study history.
examples.fix: She is interested in studying history.

examples.text: It is hard to refuse help.

units.title: Sentence combining and punctuation
units.intro: Clear punctuation prevents run-ons and fragments in exam essays.

cards.title: Avoiding run-ons and comma splices
rule: Two independent clauses need a full stop, semicolon, or conjunction: *It rained. We stayed in.* / *It rained; we stayed in.* / *It rained, so we stayed in.*
A **comma splice** joins two full sentences with only a comma — fix it.
Fragments lack a main clause: *While waiting for the bus.* → complete it.

examples.text: It rained, so we stayed in.
It rained, we stayed in.
examples.fix: It rained, so we stayed in. / It rained; we stayed in.

examples.text: While waiting for the bus, we revised notes.

cards.title: Forms and examples
head: Problem

cards.title: Useful combining tools
rule: Coordinators: *and, but, or, so, yet*
Subordinators: *because, although, when, if, while*
Semicolon + conjunctive adverb: *however, therefore, meanwhile*

examples.text: Although the test was hard, she scored well.

examples.fix: Although the test was hard, she scored well.

examples.text: The lights failed; however, the exam continued.
